answers.answer: Histones are classified in SCOPe under class a (all-alpha proteins), fold a.22 (Histone-fold), in superfamily a.22.1 (Histone-fold). The fold is defined by a three-helix core (alpha1-loop-alpha2-loop-alpha3) that pairs head-to-tail with a second histone-fold chain to form a handshake dimer. Within the superfamily, the core nucleosome histones H2A, H2B, H3 and H4 are the best-known members. Other members that share this superfamily, and therefore probable common evolutionary origin, include: archaeal histones (HMf/HMfB-type), which form histone-like dimers and tetramers; the NF-Y subunits NF-YB and NF-YC (HAP3/HAP5 in yeast), which bind CCAAT boxes as heterodimers with NF-YA; the TFIID components TAF6/TAF9 and TAF4/TAF12, which form histone-fold pairs; the CENP-S/CENP-X (MHF1/MHF2) histone-fold pair in the centromeric and FANCM-associated complex; and the DRAP1 (NC2-alpha) and NC2-beta histone-fold pair of the NC2/Dr1 repressor. Relationship strength: these share the fold and, in SCOPe, are grouped at superfamily level, which implies probable common ancestry; they are not in the same family, so they should not be treated as close homologs, and sequence identity between them is generally low. Fold-level similarity alone (e.g., to unrelated proteins with a helical bundle) does not imply homology. Important limits: (1) Membership of a histone-fold partner in a.22.1 does not transfer nucleosome or chromatin function: NF-Y, TAFs, CENP-S/X and NC2 act in transcription or kinetochore/repair complexes, and their histone-fold dimers have different partners and DNA-binding surfaces. (2) Linker histone H1/H5 is not a histone-fold protein; its globular domain is a winged-helix domain (SCOPe fold a.4, winged helix, assigned at the superfamily level), so it is not a fold-level relative of the core histones. (3) Bacterial HU and IHF are often called 'histone-like' but are not histone-fold proteins; they belong to a different all-alpha/beta DNA-binding fold (SCOPe class a, fold a.55, IHF-like DNA-binding proteins). (4) When choosing representatives for analysis, pick one per family (e.g., one core histone per type, one NF-Y, one TAF pair) rather than many near-identical sequences, and verify the current family and superfamily assignments in the SCOPe release used, because family numbering changes between releases; I could not check the release offline, so the exact family numbers are not given here.
